newsitem.title: UK: Gazprom may have to give up gas monopoly - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom may have to give up gas monopoly - analyst.

text.p: Cash-strapped Russian gas monopoly Gazprom may be forced to surrender control over domestic gas production or transportation in order to attract much-needed western investment, an industry analyst said on Thursday.
Gazprom controls 33 percent of world gas reserves but is struggling with the problem of non-payment of bills by consumers in Russia and the former Soviet republics.
The company needs capital from the West to develop new export projects said Ben van Gils, partner and member of the energy steering group at Ernst and Young International.
"Gazprom has always had a monopoly on production and transportation of gas. The question is whether it can keep this monopoly," he told a conference in London.
"It cannot do both - develop reserves and pay for the pipeline system, he said.

Van Gils said that Gazprom would like to attract western oil company investment to develop small gas fields in Siberia. But in order to attract capital, the Russian giant, which pumped over 550 billion cubic metres of gas last year, may have to offer production opportunities to foreign firms at larger fields.
"Western investors are not very interested in smaller fields. They want to go to the larger fields where the cash flow is," van Gils said.
"Gazprom would like to keep absolute control but this may not be possible."
And the price to pay for western investment in Gazprom's huge 145,000 km pipeline infrastructure may be a limited form of third party access (TPA).
"It might well be possible that large western investors might be able to force TPA in Russia. TPA is not simply a nono," van Gils said.
Gazprom is seeking to boost exports to fast-growing western European markets, through the development of new reserves on Siberia's Yamal peninsula and the expansion of pipeline capacity.
"The (pipeline system) is the jewel in the crown, so this is a very tricky area for Gazprom, said van Gils.

But Adam Whitmore, senior consultant at London Economics, said that while small amounts of gas may start moving independently in the system, Gazprom is unlikely to allow the sort of TPA seen in the British and U.S. markets.
A second foreign issue of Gazprom shares may also be on the cards to raise capital, van Gils said.
"The first issue was successful so why not another one?" he asked.
He said over $400 million was raised from the first issue which went mainly toward payment of back taxes.
Gazprom is the world's largest gas producer, accounting for about one quarter of world gas output.
